---
title: "Where do viruses hide?"
subtitle: "They're everywhere, but tiny."
---

[District 3]{.district}

## The short answer

::: block
From the Antarctic ice, the deep sea and every gram of soil to your fingernail.
Nobody has yet looked into an ecosystem and found it free of them.

The human body is one of those ecosystems, and it is the one this book is about.
:::

::: fig-pending
**The viral world.** Viruses are everywhere in the body and outnumber
everything else, but they are tiny, and larger things crowd the frame.
:::

::: block
But being everywhere does not make them easy to find:

[Most of what you sequence isn't viral.]{.claim}
:::

## Why isn't most of it viral?

::: block
Today the most common way to study viral diversity and discover new viruses is
shotgun metagenomic sequencing. But shotgun is not virus-specific: it reads
every nucleic acid in the sample, and viral genomes are a small minority of what
is there. In a stool sample, for example, bacterial, host and dietary sequences
vastly outnumber viral ones.

And a virus carries very little of it. Tens of kilobases against the few
megabases of the bacterium it infects. Abundance is counted in particles;
sequencing is counted in bases.
:::

![What a stool sequencing library is made of.](../assets/img/where/stool-composition.svg){#fig-stool fig-alt="A colon, coloured along its length: almost all of it is bacterial and dietary background, with a small viral fraction and a host fraction at the end."}

::: insight
This is one of the biggest challenges in exploring a human virome. You will see
the techniques for dealing with it in the [How-to district](how-to.qmd).
:::

## Does it change with the body site?

::: block
Have you ever seen a tiger at the North Pole, or a baobab growing in
Switzerland? Living things belong to specific ecosystems, decided by their
physiology and their evolution. The microorganisms are no different, viruses
included.

The human body is not one habitat but many. The gut is warm, crowded and without
oxygen; the skin is dry, salty and exposed. Different conditions, different
diversity (richness and abundance).
:::

## Is the site the whole story?

::: block
Would you expect someone born in the United States, eating a classic Western
diet, to carry the same viruses as someone living in the Amazon on an Indigenous
diet? Intuitively, no: lifestyle, diet, age and geography all shape these
communities. But even two people living under the same roof may carry different
ones, because of something as simple as what they eat or who they spend their
days with.

This is worth holding on to before you design an experiment, because host
ecology will either strengthen your conclusions or undermine them, depending on
whether you planned for it. So here is the whole landscape at once: which
variables move with the ecology of the host, and how much they actually move.
:::

## What other barriers are there?

::: block
A bias that is easy to miss: what has never been sequenced cannot be in the
database you classify against. Sequencing has spread a great deal, but when
444,829 public human microbiome samples were catalogued in 2021, 71.2% of those
with an identifiable origin came from Europe, the US and Canada; 46.8% from the
US alone, a country holding 4.3% of the world's population.

That gap is not only scientific. It tracks funding and infrastructure, which
means the populations missing from the reference are usually the ones with least
access to the sequencing that would put them in it.

For viromes the gap is wider still. A 2025 Chinese gut virus catalogue checked
its 93,462 viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs) against four existing
references and found 73.2% of them absent. An atlas of six sites across four
African countries recovered 40,135 viral genomes unknown to the reference,
alongside 1,005 prokaryotic ones, from the same samples and the same pipeline.
Those are different units measured against references of very different sizes,
so the ratio means little. The direction does not: the bacterial side of that
data was largely described already, and the viral side was not.

The consequence is concrete. A library from an under-represented population will
leave a larger unclassified fraction than one from a well-sampled population.
That is not your pipeline failing, and it belongs in your conclusions.
:::

::: block
The map below counts what was public in 2021. Burkina Faso appears on it with 17
samples; the African atlas has since added 384 from one site alone.
:::

::: insight
All of this is ecology. A person is an ecosystem, and ecosystems move when small
things change — a course of antibiotics, a move to a city, a different diet.
When your subjects are people, their circumstances are not context around the
study. They are variables in it, and they belong in the design.
:::

::: fivi
![](../assets/img/fivi-thinking.png){fig-alt="Fivi, thinking."}

**How you pull me out depends on what I'm made of and how I live.** There is no
single recovery protocol — which steps you need is decided by the genome I carry
and the state I'm in. That's the [How-to district](how-to.qmd).
:::
